title: What ships with a shutter, and why it ships together
author: Böss Group
excerpt: A shutter leaves the plant as a set: slat, guide, barrel, spring, operator, latch and control. The reason is not convenience. Parts specified against each other hold a cycle count that parts bought separately do not.
body: A shutter is quoted and shipped as a set — slat, bottom rail, guides and brackets, barrel, balance springs, operator with its control box, and the latch. Not because it is tidier to buy in one order, but because the numbers only hold that way.

Take the operator. Its capacity is matched to the weighed curtain, not to the area of the opening, because weight is what loads a motor. Change the slat gauge after the motor is chosen and the figure stops meaning anything. The same goes for the springs: they are wound against a curtain of known mass, and a heavier slat on the same spring puts the extra load through the motor every cycle for the life of the door.

Billet is bought in, and the slat, the guide and the bottom rail come off the same alloy and the same coating line. A guide from one supplier and a slat from another will fit; they will also wear at different rates, and the door will start to sound wrong about a year before anything actually fails.

The parts that carry the engineering are the ones nobody sees: the automatic latch that throws as the curtain lands and needs no supply of its own, the rolling-code handset, and the felt and rubber seals in the guides. All three are specified with the curtain rather than added to it.
